questions.stem: Long-term PPI use can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency. What is the mechanism?
options: PPIs increase bacterial degradation of B12 in the terminal ileum
PPIs block active transport of B12 in the terminal ileum
PPIs directly bind and inactivate intrinsic factor
Reduced gastric acid impairs cleavage of B12 from dietary proteins
explanations: Incorrect — increased bacterial degradation of B12 is not the mechanism described for PPI-associated B12 deficiency in these notes.
Incorrect — PPIs are not described as blocking active transport of B12 in the terminal ileum; the deficiency arises earlier, from impaired acid-mediated release of B12 from food.
Incorrect — PPIs work by inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase in parietal cells, not by directly binding intrinsic factor.

Correct — hydrogen ion (gastric acid) is required to cleave vitamin B12 from dietary proteins before it can be absorbed; by suppressing acid secretion, PPIs impair this step and can lead to B12 deficiency with long-term use.
questions.overview: Long-term PPI use can cause several nutrient deficiencies through reduced gastric acidity: B12 deficiency (acid is needed to cleave B12 from dietary proteins), hypomagnesemia (reduced absorption), and increased hip fracture risk (reduced calcium absorption), as well as increased risk of C. difficile infection and pneumonia from loss of the acid barrier against pathogens.

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have intestines herniating through the umbilical cord, covered by a peritoneal membrane. Which of the following is most likely true of this infant?
options: High likelihood of associated genetic abnormalities such as trisomy 21
Defect is typically located lateral to the umbilicus, not covered by peritoneum
Rarely associated with cardiac or other congenital defects
Poor gastrointestinal function is typical, with a good prognosis once function is restored
explanations: Correct — omphalocele, in which bowel herniates through the umbilical cord and remains covered by a peritoneal membrane, is associated with many genetic defects including trisomy 21, 18, and 13, as well as congenital heart defects (up to 50%), orofacial clefts, and neural tube defects.
Incorrect — this describes gastroschisis, which is a paraumbilical defect not covered by peritoneum, usually on the right side of the umbilicus.
Incorrect — omphalocele is associated with many extra-intestinal congenital conditions, including cardiac defects in up to half of cases, the opposite of what this option states.
Incorrect — this describes gastroschisis, which typically has poor GI function but a good prognosis once function is restored and has few associated congenital anomalies.
questions.overview: Omphalocele is persistence of the normal physiologic midgut herniation, with bowel covered by a peritoneal membrane through the umbilical cord, normal GI function, and strong associations with trisomies and congenital heart, orofacial, and neural tube defects. Gastroschisis is a paraumbilical abdominal wall defect (usually right-sided) with exposed, uncovered bowel, often poor GI function but few associated anomalies, and a good prognosis once bowel function is restored.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with alcohol use disorder presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Labs show an elevated lipase level and a low serum calcium level.
options: Saponification of fat by free fatty acids released from lipase-mediated triglyceride breakdown, binding calcium
Decreased PTH secretion due to systemic inflammation
Dilutional effect from massive IV fluid resuscitation
Renal loss of calcium from acute tubular necrosis
Chelation of calcium by activated trypsin
explanations: Correct — fat necrosis surrounding the inflamed pancreas releases free fatty acids (via lipase) that bind calcium in a process called saponification, forming "calcium soaps"; low calcium is a poor prognostic indicator reflecting extensive fat necrosis.
Incorrect — decreased PTH secretion from inflammation is not the mechanism described for pancreatitis-associated hypocalcemia.
Incorrect — dilution from IV fluids is not the described mechanism of hypocalcemia in pancreatitis.
Incorrect — renal calcium loss from ATN is not the described mechanism of this complication.
Incorrect — trypsin activates other pancreatic proenzymes and drives autodigestion, but it is not described as directly chelating calcium.
questions.overview: Acute pancreatitis complications include fat necrosis, which can cause hypocalcemia through saponification — free fatty acids released by lipase-mediated triglyceride breakdown bind calcium to form insoluble calcium soaps. A low calcium level is a poor prognostic sign, suggesting extensive peripancreatic fat involvement, and hypocalcemia is one component tracked in severity scoring systems like Ranson's criteria.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pruritus that is worse at night for several months. She has no history of alcohol use or viral hepatitis. Labs show markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase, mildly elevated AST/ALT, and elevated total cholesterol. Abdominal imaging shows no evidence of biliary obstruction.
explanations: Incorrect — p-ANCA is seen in up to 80% of primary sclerosing cholangitis patients (and vasculitides), not classically the hallmark antibody here.
Incorrect — anti-smooth muscle antibody is more specific for autoimmune hepatitis, not this condition.
Incorrect — anti-nuclear antibodies are seen in about 70% of these patients but are far less specific than anti-mitochondrial antibodies.

Correct — anti-mitochondrial antibodies are the hallmark of primary biliary cirrhosis, present in approximately 95% of patients, and along with markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase support the diagnosis.
Incorrect — anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody is used to diagnose celiac disease, an unrelated small bowel disorder.
questions.overview: Primary biliary cirrhosis is an autoimmune disease with T-cell attack on small intralobular bile ducts, typically presenting in women with fatigue and pruritus (often worse at night) before jaundice develops. Diagnosis relies on markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase, positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies (~95% of patients), and imaging that excludes extrahepatic biliary obstruction; treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and a palpable, non-tender, enlarged gallbladder on exam. This finding is most classically associated with which condition?
explanations: Incorrect — a common bile duct stone typically causes painful biliary obstruction, and chronic gallbladder fibrosis from prior stone disease often prevents the gallbladder from distending.
Incorrect — acute cholecystitis presents with painful RUQ tenderness and a positive Murphy's sign, not painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder.

Correct — Courvoisier's sign (painless jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder) is the classic physical exam finding for pancreatic cancer, in which slow, gradual biliary obstruction by the tumor allows the gallbladder to distend without triggering pain or acute inflammation.
Incorrect — PBC is an intrahepatic process and does not classically produce a palpable, enlarged gallbladder.
questions.overview: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, most commonly arising in the pancreatic head, classically presents with "painless jaundice" due to slow, gradual bile duct obstruction, along with Courvoisier's sign (a palpable, non-tender, distended gallbladder) and sometimes Trousseau's syndrome (migratory superficial thrombophlebitis from a hypercoagulable state). Prognosis is very poor, and CA-19-9 is a tumor marker used to monitor disease rather than for initial diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the initial activation of trypsinogen to trypsin in the small intestine?
options: Trypsin itself, without any other activator
explanations: Incorrect — while active trypsin can further activate more trypsinogen once present, the initial activation step requires enterokinase at the brush border.
Incorrect — chymotrypsin is itself activated by trypsin (from chymotrypsinogen), not an activator of trypsinogen.
Incorrect — pepsin functions in the stomach to digest proteins and is not involved in activating pancreatic trypsinogen in the small intestine.

Correct — trypsinogen is secreted by the pancreas in an inactive form and is normally activated at the intestinal brush border by enterokinase (enteropeptidase); once activated, trypsin then activates all the other pancreatic protein-digesting proenzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) as well as more trypsinogen.
questions.overview: Pancreatic acinar cells secrete protein-digesting enzymes as inactive zymogens to prevent autodigestion of the pancreas. Trypsinogen is the key zymogen, activated at the intestinal brush border by enterokinase; the resulting trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidase, as well as additional trypsinogen — and dysregulated premature activation of this cascade within the pancreas is the central mechanism of acute pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A healthy 22-year-old develops mild scleral icterus during final exams week and after a viral illness. Total bilirubin is 2.5 mg/dL, predominantly unconjugated, with otherwise normal liver function tests. What is the most likely underlying defect?
options: Autoimmune destruction of bile duct epithelium
Defective canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin
explanations: Incorrect — autoimmune destruction of bile ducts describes primary biliary cirrhosis, a distinct disease with cholestatic lab findings, not the isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia of Gilbert's syndrome.

Incorrect — complete or severely reduced UGT activity describes Crigler-Najjar syndrome, which causes much higher bilirubin levels and risk of kernicterus, not the mild, benign presentation described here.

Correct — Gilbert's syndrome results from a mild decrease in UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT) function, typically due to a defective gene promoter, causing mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually <3 mg/dL) that can be triggered by fasting, illness, stress, or exertion, with no serious clinical consequences.
Incorrect — defective excretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile describes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not the mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia seen here.
questions.overview: Gilbert's syndrome is a common, benign condition caused by a mild reduction in UDP-glucuronyltransferase activity, leading to mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually under 3 mg/dL) that becomes more apparent during fasting, illness, stress, or exertion. It has no serious clinical consequences, in contrast to Crigler-Najjar syndrome, which involves severely reduced or absent enzyme activity and can cause kernicterus.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old presents with new-onset tremor, dysarthria, and behavioral changes along with elevated liver enzymes. Slit lamp exam reveals brownish rings at the corneal limbus. Labs show a low serum ceruloplasmin level.
explanations: Incorrect — alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver cirrhosis and emphysema through abnormal protein polymerization, not copper accumulation.

Correct — Wilson's disease is caused by mutation of ATP7B, which normally incorporates copper into ceruloplasmin and excretes copper into bile; loss of function causes copper accumulation in the liver and other tissues (brain, cornea), low serum ceruloplasmin, and neuropsychiatric and hepatic disease, with Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit lamp exam.
Incorrect — mutation of the HFE protein/gene causes hereditary hemochromatosis, a disorder of iron (not copper) metabolism.
Incorrect — deficiency of this enzyme causes Gilbert's or Crigler-Najjar syndrome, disorders of bilirubin conjugation, not copper metabolism.
Incorrect — defective multidrug resistance protein causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome (impaired conjugated bilirubin excretion), not copper accumulation.
questions.overview: Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of ATP7B, the hepatic copper transport protein, resulting in impaired biliary copper excretion and reduced incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin. Copper accumulates in the liver (cirrhosis, risk of HCC) and deposits in the brain (basal ganglia — causing Parkinsonian movement disorders, dysarthria, dementia) and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings); diagnosis relies on low ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper excretion, and treatment is penicillamine.

questions.stem: During emergency surgery for liver trauma, a surgeon clamps a ligament connecting the liver to the duodenum to control bleeding (Pringle maneuver). Which structure is NOT contained within the clamped ligament?
explanations: Incorrect — the proper hepatic artery is one of the three structures contained within the hepatoduodenal ligament.

Correct — the hepatoduodenal ligament clamped during a Pringle maneuver contains the proper hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct, but not the IVC; if bleeding continues despite clamping, the source is the IVC or hepatic veins.
Incorrect — the common bile duct is one of the three structures contained within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
Incorrect — the portal vein is one of the three structures contained within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.overview: The hepatoduodenal ligament, part of the lesser omentum, contains the proper hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct. The Pringle maneuver — clamping this ligament — is used to control liver hemorrhage; if bleeding persists despite clamping, the source is likely the IVC or hepatic veins, which lie outside the ligament.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with a known metastatic small intestinal carcinoid tumor to the liver presents with episodic flushing, watery diarrhea, and a new tricuspid regurgitation murmur.
explanations: Incorrect — HVA is a dopamine metabolite associated with neuroblastoma, not carcinoid syndrome.
Incorrect — porphobilinogen is elevated in acute porphyrias, unrelated to carcinoid syndrome.

Correct — 5-HIAA is the metabolite of serotonin, measured in a 24-hour urine collection to diagnose carcinoid syndrome, which occurs when a carcinoid tumor (usually metastatic to the liver, bypassing hepatic serotonin inactivation) secretes excess serotonin causing flushing, diarrhea, and fibrotic valvular heart disease (typically right-sided, since serotonin is inactivated by the lungs before reaching the left heart).
Incorrect — VMA is a catecholamine metabolite used to diagnose pheochromocytoma, not carcinoid syndrome.
Incorrect — metanephrines are also catecholamine metabolites used for pheochromocytoma diagnosis, not carcinoid syndrome.
questions.overview: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine tumors, most commonly arising in the small intestine, that secrete serotonin; carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, fibrotic valvular heart disease) only occurs once tumor secretions bypass hepatic and pulmonary metabolism, typically after liver metastasis. Diagnosis relies on elevated urinary 5-HIAA (a serotonin metabolite), and right-sided (tricuspid/pulmonic) valve lesions predominate because serotonin is inactivated in the lungs before reaching the left heart; treatment includes surgical resection and octreotide.

questions.stem: A child presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and failure to thrive. Duodenal biopsy shows blunting of villi, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which antibody has the highest diagnostic accuracy for this condition (when IgA levels are normal)?
explanations: Correct — IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (along with IgA anti-endomysial antibody) has the highest diagnostic accuracy for celiac disease and is used as an automated screening test; IgG-based testing is used when a patient has coexisting IgA deficiency.
Incorrect — anti-mitochondrial antibody is the hallmark of primary biliary cirrhosis, an unrelated liver disease.
Incorrect — anti-gliadin antibody testing is rarely used because of its poor diagnostic accuracy compared to other celiac serologies.
Incorrect — anti-smooth muscle antibody is associated with autoimmune hepatitis, not celiac disease.
questions.overview: Celiac disease is a T-cell-mediated (type IV hypersensitivity) autoimmune reaction to deamidated gliadin, associated with HLA-DQ2/DQ8, that causes villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and lamina propria lymphocytosis, most prominently in the duodenum. IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (and anti-endomysial) antibodies have the highest diagnostic accuracy, and treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet; dermatitis herpetiformis is an associated skin finding.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man reports several months of progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids from the onset, along with regurgitation of undigested food and bad breath. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth narrowing at the distal end ("bird's beak"). Esophageal manometry shows failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation with increased LES tone.
options: Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus of the lower esophagus
Metaplasia of esophageal squamous epithelium to columnar epithelium
Decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone due to smooth muscle atrophy, as in scleroderma
Formation of a false diverticulum at Killian's triangle
Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells with loss of intrinsic factor
explanations: Correct — achalasia results from loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, causing failure of LES relaxation, increased LES tone, dysphagia to both solids and liquids, and a "bird's beak" on barium swallow.
Incorrect — squamous-to-columnar metaplasia describes Barrett's esophagus, a consequence of chronic GERD, not achalasia.
Incorrect — this describes scleroderma, which causes decreased LES tone (the opposite of achalasia's increased LES tone) and is distinguished from achalasia on manometry.
Incorrect — this describes Zenker's diverticulum, which causes dysphagia and halitosis but arises from cricopharyngeal dysfunction at the pharyngoesophageal junction, not the LES.
Incorrect — this describes autoimmune (pernicious anemia) gastritis, an unrelated condition affecting vitamin B12 absorption, not esophageal motility.
questions.overview: Achalasia is caused by loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, leading to failure of LES relaxation and increased LES tone; causes include idiopathic disease and Chagas disease. It presents with dysphagia to both solids and liquids (distinguishing it from mechanical obstruction), and is diagnosed by barium swallow ("bird's beak") and manometry, which shows increased LES tone — the opposite of the decreased tone seen in scleroderma.

questions.stem: A young adult has hundreds of colonic adenomatous polyps on colonoscopy and a strong family history of colon cancer at a young age. Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation. Which gene is mutated?
explanations: Incorrect — K-RAS mutation is a later, somatic step in the chromosomal instability (adenoma-carcinoma) pathway of sporadic colon cancer, not the germline mutation causing FAP.

Correct — FAP is caused by a germline mutation of the APC tumor suppressor gene (chromosome 5q), which normally prevents accumulation of β-catenin; loss of APC function leads to widespread colonic polyps with essentially 100% progression to colon cancer, requiring prophylactic colectomy.

Incorrect — mismatch repair gene mutations cause hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) via microsatellite instability, a distinct pathway from FAP's chromosomal instability/APC pathway.
Incorrect — the DCC gene is a tumor suppressor frequently mutated in advanced colorectal cancers, not the causative germline mutation in FAP.
questions.overview: Familial adenomatous polyposis is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a germline APC gene mutation, leading to hundreds of colonic adenomatous polyps and essentially universal progression to colon cancer, necessitating colectomy. It follows the chromosomal instability (adenoma-carcinoma sequence) pathway, in which APC loss is followed by K-RAS mutation and then p53 loss — distinct from the microsatellite instability pathway underlying Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation) presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain. On exam, she has only mild abdominal tenderness with no rebound or guarding, despite the severity of her pain. Labs show leukocytosis, elevated lactate, and metabolic acidosis.
options: Chronic narrowing of the IMA causing intestinal angina
Non-occlusive ischemia from hypoperfusion affecting the splenic flexure
Arterial thrombosis at a site of atherosclerosis in the celiac trunk
Venous thrombosis of the mesenteric vein due to hypercoagulability
Embolism to the SMA from a left atrial appendage thrombus
explanations: Incorrect — chronic IMA narrowing causes intestinal angina, a chronic recurrent postprandial pain syndrome in patients with vascular disease, not this acute presentation.
Incorrect — non-occlusive ischemia from hypoperfusion (shock) typically affects colonic watershed areas like the splenic flexure, not the jejunum, and there's no history of shock here.

Incorrect — arterial thrombosis occurs at a site of pre-existing atherosclerosis in a patient with known vascular disease, and involves the SMA (supplying the midgut), not the celiac trunk in this context.
Incorrect — venous thrombosis is associated with hypercoagulable states or malignancy, which are not indicated in this patient's history.

Correct — embolism is the most common cause of acute mesenteric ischemia, often originating from a cardiac source such as a left atrial appendage thrombus in atrial fibrillation, and it often affects the jejunum via the SMA.
questions.overview: Acute mesenteric ischemia is most commonly caused by arterial embolism, often from a cardiac source (LV thrombus, atrial fibrillation), and classically affects the jejunum via the SMA. Other causes include arterial thrombosis at atherosclerotic sites, mesenteric venous thrombosis (hypercoagulable states), and non-occlusive ischemia from shock (affecting colonic watershed areas). The classic exam finding is pain out of proportion to exam, with only mild tenderness and no peritoneal signs, plus elevated lactate and leukocytosis.

questions.stem: A newborn fails to pass meconium within 48 hours and has abdominal distention. Rectal suction biopsy shows absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses. What is the embryologic basis of this disease?
options: Failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate
Failure of recanalization of the bowel lumen
Abnormal rotation of the midgut around the SMA
Failure of neural crest cell migration to the distal colon
explanations: Incorrect — failure of vitelline duct obliteration leads to Meckel's diverticulum or related anomalies, not Hirschsprung's disease.
Incorrect — failure of recanalization causes intestinal atresia (e.g., duodenal atresia), a distinct congenital anomaly from Hirschsprung's disease.
Incorrect — abnormal midgut rotation causes malrotation and potential volvulus, not the absence of ganglion cells seen in Hirschsprung's disease.

Correct — Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of neural crest cell migration to the distal colon, leading to absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner's) and myenteric (Auerbach's) plexuses, causing loss of peristalsis and functional obstruction; the rectum is always involved, so diagnosis requires rectal suction biopsy.
questions.overview: Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital motor disorder of the colon caused by failure of neural crest cell migration, resulting in absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the distal colon (always including the rectum), which prevents normal peristalsis. It presents with failure to pass meconium and abdominal distention, is associated with Down syndrome, and is diagnosed by rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells, with treatment by surgical resection of the aganglionic segment.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has recurrent peptic ulcers in the distal duodenum and jejunum, refractory to standard proton pump inhibitor therapy, along with chronic diarrhea that improves somewhat with food. Fasting serum gastrin level is markedly elevated (>10 times normal). Administration of secretin causes a further rise in his gastrin level.
options: Antral G-cell hyperplasia from chronic H. pylori infection
explanations: Incorrect — pernicious anemia causes elevated gastrin due to loss of acid feedback inhibition (achlorhydria), but does not cause refractory ulcers or diarrhea, and would not show a paradoxical secretin response.

Correct — Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor, producing markedly elevated fasting gastrin, refractory ulcers in the distal duodenum/jejunum, diarrhea from excess acid, and a paradoxical rise in gastrin after secretin (unlike normal G cells, which are inhibited by secretin).
Incorrect — VIPoma causes watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and achlorhydria ("WDHA syndrome"), not ulcers or elevated gastrin.

Incorrect — H. pylori can increase gastrin release, but it does not produce the markedly elevated (>10x normal) gastrin level or the paradoxical rise in gastrin with secretin that is characteristic of a gastrinoma.
Incorrect — somatostatinoma is not associated with elevated gastrin or ulcer disease in these notes.
questions.overview: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) of the duodenum or pancreas, causing excessive acid secretion that leads to refractory ulcers (often distal to the duodenal bulb or in the jejunum), diarrhea, and mucosal hypertrophy. Diagnosis relies on a markedly elevated fasting gastrin level and a secretin stimulation test, which paradoxically increases gastrin in gastrinoma (unlike normal G cells, which are suppressed by secretin).

questions.stem: A structure located above the pectinate line drains lymphatically to which of the following?
explanations: Incorrect — superficial inguinal nodes drain structures below the pectinate line, not above it.

Correct — structures above the pectinate line (derived from hindgut) drain lymphatically to the internal iliac nodes, are supplied by the superior rectal artery, and give rise to internal hemorrhoids, which have visceral (painless) innervation.
Incorrect — para-aortic nodes are not described as the drainage site for this region in these notes.
Incorrect — celiac nodes drain foregut structures, not the anorectal region above the pectinate line.
questions.overview: The pectinate (dentate) line divides the anal canal into a hindgut-derived proximal portion (columnar epithelium, superior rectal artery, internal iliac lymph nodes, visceral/painless innervation, internal hemorrhoids, adenocarcinoma risk) and an ectoderm-derived distal portion (stratified squamous epithelium, inferior rectal artery, superficial inguinal lymph nodes, somatic/painful innervation, external hemorrhoids, squamous cell carcinoma risk). This distinction explains why internal hemorrhoids are painless while external hemorrhoids are painful.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man who smokes presents with a painless, mobile mass in the parotid gland. Biopsy shows cystic spaces filled with fluid, surrounded by dense lymphoid tissue with germinal centers. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect — sialadenitis is inflammation of the salivary gland, usually secondary to an obstructing stone and bacterial infection, not a neoplasm.
Incorrect — mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant salivary tumor, composed of a mixture of squamous and mucus-secreting cells, and is associated with prior radiation, not smoking.

Correct — Warthin's tumor is the second most common salivary gland tumor, occurs in the parotid gland, is strongly associated with smoking (8x more common), and shows cysts surrounded by dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centers on histology.
Incorrect — pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary tumor overall, composed of epithelial and stromal (sometimes cartilage) tissue, not the cystic/lymphoid histology described.
questions.overview: Warthin's tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum) is the second most common salivary gland tumor, occurring almost exclusively in the parotid gland, with smoking as a strong risk factor (8-fold increase). Histologically it shows fluid-filled cysts surrounded by dense lymphoid tissue with germinal centers, distinguishing it from pleomorphic adenoma (epithelial and stromal/cartilage tissue) and mucoepidermoid carcinoma (mixed squamous and mucous cells, associated with radiation exposure).

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with a recent influenza B infection is given aspirin for fever and subsequently develops vomiting, altered mental status, and hepatomegaly with fatty changes on liver biopsy. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect — alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a chronic inherited condition causing cirrhosis and emphysema, not an acute presentation following aspirin use during a viral illness.
Incorrect — acetaminophen toxicity causes acute liver failure through NAPQI accumulation after an overdose, unrelated to aspirin use or a preceding viral infection.

Correct — Reye's syndrome occurs in children given aspirin during a viral infection (classically varicella zoster or influenza B), causing mitochondrial damage, fatty liver changes, hepatomegaly, and encephalopathy (vomiting, coma); aspirin should be avoided in children except in Kawasaki disease.
Incorrect — Wilson's disease is a chronic inherited disorder of copper metabolism, not an acute illness triggered by aspirin and viral infection.
questions.overview: Reye's syndrome is a rare, often fatal cause of acute liver failure and encephalopathy in children who take aspirin during a viral infection (classically varicella or influenza B); aspirin is thought to inhibit mitochondrial beta-oxidation, causing fatty liver changes, vomiting, and progression to coma. This is why aspirin is avoided in children except for specific indications like Kawasaki disease.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis undergoes paracentesis for new ascites. Serum albumin is 3.5 g/dL and ascitic fluid albumin is 1.5 g/dL. What does the calculated SAAG value indicate?
options: SAAG <1.1 g/dL, consistent with portal hypertension
SAAG <1.1 g/dL, consistent with malignant ascites
SAAG >1.1 g/dL, consistent with portal hypertension
explanations: Incorrect — while portal hypertension is the correct clinical correlation, the SAAG value itself is above, not below, 1.1 g/dL.
Incorrect — the calculated SAAG (3.5 - 1.5 = 2.0 g/dL) is greater than, not less than, 1.1 g/dL, and a value below 1.1 would suggest malignant (leaky vasculature) ascites, not this scenario.

Correct — SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin = 3.5 minus 1.5 = 2.0 g/dL, which is greater than 1.1 g/dL; a high SAAG indicates a large gradient driven by portal hypertension pushing fluid (but not albumin) into the peritoneal cavity, consistent with this patient's cirrhosis.

Incorrect — a SAAG greater than 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension, not malignancy; malignant ascites is associated with a SAAG below 1.1 g/dL due to leaky vasculature allowing albumin into the peritoneal fluid.
questions.overview: The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) helps distinguish the cause of new or worsening ascites: a SAAG greater than 1.1 g/dL reflects a high-pressure state (portal hypertension) driving protein-poor fluid into the peritoneum, while a SAAG less than 1.1 g/dL suggests leaky vasculature from malignancy, allowing albumin to enter the ascitic fluid alongside water.

questions.stem: Long-standing GERD leads to a histologic change in the distal esophagus in which the normal epithelium is replaced by a new epithelial type containing goblet cells. What is this epithelial transformation?
options: Non-keratinized squamous epithelium to non-ciliated columnar (intestinal) epithelium
Squamous epithelium to gastric-type simple columnar epithelium without goblet cells
explanations: Incorrect — transitional epithelium is not part of normal esophageal or gastric histology and is not relevant to this metaplastic change.

Correct — Barrett's esophagus is metaplasia of the normal non-keratinized squamous epithelium of the esophagus into non-ciliated columnar (intestinal-type) epithelium containing goblet cells, occurring as a consequence of long-standing GERD.
Incorrect — the metaplastic epithelium in Barrett's esophagus is intestinal-type and characteristically contains goblet cells, which distinguish it from simple gastric-type columnar epithelium.
Incorrect — this describes the reverse of the actual direction of metaplasia seen in Barrett's esophagus.
questions.overview: Barrett's esophagus develops from long-standing GERD, in which chronic acid exposure causes metaplasia of the normal non-keratinized squamous esophageal epithelium into intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells. It is a precursor lesion for esophageal adenocarcinoma (typically in the lower third of the esophagus), so patients undergo surveillance endoscopy with biopsy.

questions.stem: H. pylori is able to survive in the acidic gastric environment primarily through which mechanism?
options: Secretion of a protective mucous capsule impermeable to acid
Production of catalase to neutralize gastric acid
Rapid replication that outpaces acid-mediated killing
Production of urease, generating ammonium to neutralize local acid
explanations: Incorrect — a protective mucous capsule is not the mechanism described for H. pylori's acid resistance in these notes.
Incorrect — catalase is not the mechanism described for acid neutralization by H. pylori in these notes.
Incorrect — rapid replication is not the described survival mechanism; H. pylori actively neutralizes local acid instead.

Correct — H. pylori is urease-positive, hydrolyzing urea to produce ammonium, which locally neutralizes stomach acid and protects the bacteria, though the resulting ammonium chloride is itself damaging to the gastric mucosa; this urease activity is also exploited diagnostically in the urea breath test.
questions.overview: H. pylori is a gram-negative, urease-positive rod that colonizes the gastric antrum, causing acute and chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. Its urease enzyme hydrolyzes urea into ammonium, which neutralizes local gastric acid to allow bacterial survival (while also damaging the mucosa), and this same reaction is exploited by the diagnostic urea breath test; H. pylori is treated with triple therapy (PPI plus two antibiotics).

questions.stem: A patient with recent massive weight loss develops postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Imaging shows a portion of duodenum compressed between the aorta and an overlying artery. Which structure is compressed?
options: Third (distal transverse) portion of the duodenum
explanations: Correct — the SMA courses over the distal (third) portion of the duodenum, which lies between the aorta and the SMA; mesenteric fat normally protects the duodenum from compression, and rapid weight loss can shrink this fat pad, leading to obstruction.
Incorrect — the splenic flexure is a colonic watershed area vulnerable to ischemia in shock, not the site of SMA syndrome compression.
Incorrect — the jejunum is not the site of compression in SMA syndrome.
Incorrect — the second portion of the duodenum is not compressed in SMA syndrome; it is the third portion that lies between the aorta and SMA.
questions.overview: SMA syndrome is a rare cause of bowel obstruction in which the distal third of the duodenum, sandwiched between the aorta and the overlying SMA, becomes compressed. It classically occurs after massive, rapid weight loss, which depletes the mesenteric fat pad that normally cushions the duodenum from the artery, causing postprandial pain, nausea, and vomiting.

questions.stem: Which of the following increases the risk of cholesterol gallstone formation primarily through increased cholesterol synthesis?
explanations: Incorrect — cirrhosis decreases bile salt synthesis, another bile-salt-depletion mechanism rather than a cholesterol synthesis pathway.
Incorrect — cystic fibrosis increases cholesterol gallstone risk through fat malabsorption leading to loss of bile acids, a bile-salt-depletion mechanism, not increased cholesterol synthesis.
Incorrect — Crohn's disease causes bile salt malabsorption due to ileal inflammation, a bile-salt-depletion mechanism rather than increased cholesterol synthesis.

Correct — estrogen (from female gender, pregnancy, or multiparity) increases cholesterol synthesis and contributes to cholesterol gallstone formation; progesterone additionally slows gallbladder emptying.
questions.overview: Cholesterol gallstones form when the delicate balance of bile components is disrupted, and risk factors fall into three categories: excess estrogen (increases cholesterol synthesis; female gender, pregnancy), excess cholesterol (obesity, rapid weight loss), and loss of bile salts (cirrhosis, Crohn's disease, cystic fibrosis, bile acid resins). Risk is classically highest around age 40, and these stones are usually radiolucent on X-ray.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice. He is also confused and hypotensive. Labs show leukocytosis, a cholestatic pattern (Alk Phos >> AST/ALT), and elevated conjugated bilirubin.
explanations: Incorrect — acute cholecystitis presents with RUQ pain, fever, and a positive Murphy's sign, but not typically jaundice, confusion, or hypotension as the primary presentation.
Incorrect — gallstone pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain from pancreatic inflammation, and Ranson's criteria assess pancreatitis severity, not this cholangitis presentation.

Correct — this patient has ascending cholangitis, with biliary obstruction plus infection causing fever, pain, and jaundice (Charcot's triad); the addition of confusion and hypotension defines Reynolds pentad, indicating sepsis and shock.
Incorrect — Charcot's triad alone (without confusion/hypotension) does not capture this patient's full presentation, and PSC is a chronic autoimmune process, not an acute infectious cholangitis.

Incorrect — Courvoisier's sign (painless jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder) is classic for pancreatic cancer, not choledocholithiasis, and this patient has pain and systemic infection, not painless obstruction.
questions.overview: Ascending cholangitis occurs when a biliary stone obstructs bile flow, allowing gut bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella) to ascend the biliary tree and cause infection. Charcot's triad (fever, abdominal pain, jaundice) reflects cholestasis with infection, while the addition of confusion and hypotension (Reynolds pentad) signals sepsis and shock; treatment requires antibiotics and biliary drainage (endoscopic sphincterotomy).

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with painless rectal bleeding. Physical exam is otherwise unremarkable. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focal area of uptake in the right lower quadrant, corresponding to ectopic gastric mucosa.
options: Incomplete closure of the abdominal wall lateral to the umbilical ring
Failure of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds to fuse
Failure of recanalization of the duodenum
Persistent remnant of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
explanations: Incorrect — incomplete lateral abdominal wall closure describes gastroschisis, a ventral wall defect, not an ileal diverticulum.
Incorrect — failure of pancreatic bud fusion causes pancreas divisum, an unrelated pancreatic ductal anomaly.
Incorrect — failure of duodenal recanalization causes duodenal atresia, presenting with the "double bubble" sign, not painless rectal bleeding from an ileal outpouching.
Incorrect — a persistent processus vaginalis is the embryologic basis of an indirect inguinal hernia, not this lesion.

Correct — this is a Meckel's diverticulum, the most common congenital GI anomaly, a true diverticulum from a persistent vitelline duct remnant, often containing ectopic gastric tissue that can ulcerate and bleed; it is classically diagnosed with a technetium scan that detects the ectopic gastric mucosa.
questions.overview: Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital GI anomaly, a true diverticulum arising from a persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct remnant, often containing ectopic gastric (or pancreatic) tissue that can cause ulceration, painless bleeding, or serve as a lead point for intussusception. The "Rule of 2's" summarizes its epidemiology (2% of population, 2:1 male predominance, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, often presenting before age 2), and it is diagnosed with a technetium scan that detects ectopic gastric mucosa.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an established risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma?
options: Chronic hepatitis B or C infection
explanations: Incorrect — hepatitis A causes an acute, self-limited infection and does not lead to chronic liver disease or cirrhosis, so it is not a described risk factor for HCC.
Incorrect — Gilbert's syndrome is a benign condition with no described association with liver cancer risk.

Correct — hepatocellular carcinoma most commonly arises as a consequence of chronic liver disease, with chronic hepatitis B and C infection being major risk factors, alongside alcoholic cirrhosis, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and aflatoxin exposure.
Incorrect — gallstone disease (particularly porcelain gallbladder) is a risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma, not hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.overview: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver tumor and typically arises as a consequence of chronic liver disease — chronic hepatitis B or C, alcoholic cirrhosis, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency are established risk factors, along with dietary aflatoxin exposure from Aspergillus-contaminated food. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is used to aid diagnosis and monitor high-risk patients, though imaging and biopsy are often needed for confirmation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with several months of crampy right lower quadrant pain and non-bloody diarrhea, with weight loss and macrocytic anemia. Colonoscopy shows patchy areas of inflammation with normal-appearing mucosa in between ("skip lesions"), and biopsy reveals transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. The rectum is spared.
explanations: Incorrect — ulcerative colitis always involves the rectum, spreads continuously without skip lesions, is limited to mucosa/submucosa (not transmural), and does not form granulomas.
Incorrect — infectious colitis is typically acute and self-limited, and would not show the chronic transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas and skip lesions described here.

Correct — this presentation (RLQ pain, non-bloody diarrhea from malabsorption, macrocytic anemia from terminal ileal B12 malabsorption, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, rectal sparing) is classic for Crohn's disease.
Incorrect — ischemic colitis typically presents acutely, often in older patients with vascular risk factors or hypoperfusion, not with chronic granulomatous transmural skip lesions.
Incorrect — diverticulitis presents with acute LLQ pain and fever from an inflamed diverticulum, not chronic RLQ symptoms with granulomatous skip lesions.
questions.overview: Crohn's disease is a Th1-mediated autoimmune disease that can affect any part of the GI tract ("mouth to anus") with transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, skip lesions, and frequent rectal sparing; the terminal ileum is a common site, leading to B12 malabsorption and non-bloody diarrhea. This contrasts with ulcerative colitis, which is Th2-mediated, always involves the rectum, spreads continuously, is limited to the mucosa/submucosa, and lacks granulomas.

questions.stem: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops fatigue, pruritus, and cholestatic liver enzymes. Cholangiogram shows multifocal strictures and dilations of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts ("beading"). What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect — choledocholithiasis is a common bile duct stone causing biliary obstruction, not a chronic autoimmune stricturing process associated with UC.
Incorrect — PBC involves only intrahepatic bile ducts, is associated with Sjogren's syndrome (not UC), and is diagnosed with anti-mitochondrial antibodies rather than cholangiogram beading.
Incorrect — cholangiocarcinoma is a cancer of bile duct epithelial cells that can complicate PSC, but it does not itself describe the strictures and multifocal beading pattern seen here.

Correct — PSC is an autoimmune disorder involving inflammation, fibrosis, and strictures of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, strongly associated with ulcerative colitis (~90% of PSC patients have IBD, usually UC), and shows "beading" of ducts on cholangiogram.
questions.overview: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is an autoimmune disease causing inflammation, fibrosis, and strictures ("beading" on cholangiogram, "onion-skin" fibrosis on histology) of both intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, strongly linked to ulcerative colitis. It differs from primary biliary cirrhosis (intrahepatic ducts only, associated with Sjogren's, anti-mitochondrial antibody positive), and patients with PSC require annual screening for cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A hernia is found to originate lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and is covered by all three layers of spermatic fascia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Correct — an indirect inguinal hernia originates lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, follows the path of testicular descent through the deep and superficial inguinal rings, and is covered by all three layers of spermatic fascia, reflecting its origin from a patent processus vaginalis.
Incorrect — a direct inguinal hernia originates medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through Hesselbach's triangle, and is covered only by external spermatic fascia.
Incorrect — an umbilical hernia is a ventral hernia near the umbilicus, unrelated to the inguinal canal anatomy described.
Incorrect — a femoral hernia occurs medial to the femoral vessels, through the femoral ring below the inguinal ligament, unrelated to the inguinal canal or epigastric vessel landmarks.
questions.overview: Indirect inguinal hernias arise lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, follow the path of testicular descent through the internal and external inguinal rings, and are covered by all three spermatic fascial layers due to a persistent processus vaginalis — this is the most common type of inguinal hernia in both sexes. Direct inguinal hernias arise medial to the epigastric vessels through a weakened Hesselbach's triangle floor (transversalis fascia), typically in older men, and are covered only by external spermatic fascia.
